title: Test-Time Compute: more steps, more candidates and more structure
description: How inference compute can extend reasoning, compare candidates, search branches and change cost and latency without guaranteeing better answers by itself.

provenance.timing_basis: Candidate scene/cue boundaries compared with the exact approved decoded MP4 at every scene boundary and every cue midpoint; this validates discovery timing/content, not renderer provenance.

chapters.name: Test-Time Compute: the second scaling dimension.

cues.text: The second scaling dimension.
More steps.
More candidates.
Better compute decisions.

visual_description: Three mechanisms, sequential, parallel and structured, are revealed progressively to introduce three ways to spend more compute during inference.

chapters.name: Not only train more. Think longer.

cues.text: One lever is training: more parameters, more data and more compute to build the model.
Kaplan's scaling laws documented that relationship in 2020.
But there is a second dimension.
How much compute is spent on each individual answer.
That is test-time compute.

visual_description: Two columns separate training from inference and show that per-answer budget is distinct from the compute used to build model weights.

chapters.name: Force the model to keep thinking.

cues.text: Chain-of-thought decomposes a problem into intermediate steps.
Reasoning models can extend that process.
A technique called budget forcing suppresses the end token and adds "Wait".
In the s1-32B study, budget forcing raised AIME24 from 50% to about 57%.
More steps can improve an answer; they do not guarantee it.

visual_description: A Frame → Split → Check sequence is extended with Wait before the end token and ends with the reported AIME24 comparison, 50% → about 57%.

chapters.name: Generate many answers. Keep the best.

cues.text: Best-of-N generates several answers
and uses an evaluator to select the best one.
Another strategy is majority voting.
The selection criterion matters as much as the number of candidates.
On AIME 2024, o1 went from 74% with one sample
to 83% with consensus across 64 samples.
That is majority-based selection.

visual_description: Four candidates for 17 × 6 are evaluated and voted on; the screen then shows the reported o1 AIME 2024 comparison, 74% for one sample and 83% with consensus across 64 samples.

chapters.name: Explore branches. Prune weak ones.

cues.text: Tree search does not generate a single linear chain.
It explores multiple branches, evaluates each one and prunes the least promising.
Cost depends on how many branches are expanded.
For complex planning, it lets the system compare alternative routes before continuing.
Improvement is not automatic: it depends on the task, evaluator and search budget.

visual_description: A tree starts at the problem, expands routes A/B/C, prunes branches and keeps a selected route through Continue to illustrate exploration, evaluation and pruning.

chapters.name: Each token waits for the previous one.

cues.text: In standard autoregressive decoding, each token depends on the tokens before it.
At a fixed rate of 100 tokens per second, generating a 5,000-token chain takes 50 seconds.
Shortening the chain or generating tokens faster reduces that wait.
The sequential dependency remains.
Latency is a real design constraint.

visual_description: A row of tokens accumulates sequentially while a timeline ends in the illustrative calculation 5,000 ÷ 100 = 50 s.

chapters.name: Larger model or more time to think.

cues.text: Test-time compute and pretraining are complementary.
On some tasks, a smaller model with more inference compute can outperform a larger model with less.
Cost is no longer determined by size alone.
Efficient systems adapt both the model and the budget to each problem.
That decision requires task-level evaluation.
That is complementary scaling.

visual_description: A plane compares model size with compute per query, placing a smaller model with more inference beside a larger model to explain complementary allocation.
